target_section: How do I register on OEP?
why_new: The three-day pre-decision training at the DEMO, and one district's registration volume.

claim: The bodies of the eight Bangladeshis who died on a boat off Tunisia in February 2024 reached Dhaka's Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport on a Saudia flight on 2 May 2024, and were sent to the Dhaka Medical College morgue for post-mortem before being handed to the families.
target_section: How is the body brought home?
why_new: The bodies came home about two and a half months after the deaths, and went to a post-mortem before release to families.

claim: Ariful Haque Chowdhury MP, the Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Minister, told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that when a Bangladeshi citizen dies abroad, whether the person went by a legal or an illegal route, the government brings the body home and also gives the family financial help and help with the children's education, and that work is under way to introduce a welfare card for expatriates carrying various services.
target_section: How is the body brought home?
why_new: The minister's statement that repatriation of the body does not depend on having gone legally, and that a welfare card is being prepared (not yet issued as of August 2026).

claim: A December 2025 Prothom Alo column by Nahid Hasan works through a Saudi pest-control job: the set wage is 700 riyals a month, which he gives as Tk 22,400, so two years of eight-hour days under the contract earn Tk 5 lakh 37 thousand 600, and after about Tk 2 lakh in living costs Tk 3 lakh 37 thousand 600 is left to send home.
target_section: How long will it take to pay back what I spend?
why_new: A worked example for one named job at SR 700; the FAQ example uses SR 800.

claim: By the column's arithmetic the worker is about Tk 2 lakh 32 thousand short of recovering the cost after two years, and in effect has to double the visa period and work four years for almost no gain.
target_section: How long will it take to pay back what I spend?
why_new: The conclusion of the worked example: the first contract does not repay the cost.

claim: The Cumilla Probashi Kallyan Centre's assistant director said in April 2026 that financial help for bringing a body home is given for BMET card holders, that a free ambulance takes the body from the airport to its destination, and that Tk 25,000 is paid after the body arrives and up to Tk 3 lakh in eligible cases.
target_section: If a worker dies abroad, what does the family get?
why_new: Conflict to resolve: the guide says a Tk 35,000 cheque at the airport; this official says Tk 25,000 after the body arrives.

claim: Badrul Huda, president of the Multi-Party Advocacy Forum in Cumilla, said that information not reaching the family when someone dies or goes missing abroad is a major humanitarian problem.
target_section: If a worker dies abroad, what does the family get?
why_new: Families not being told of deaths, as raised by a local forum.

claim: The principal of the government technical training centre near the Sandwip upazila complex, Muhammad Sharfuddin, said 750 people trained there last year (2025) and about 300 trainees were currently enrolled, and according to BMET data 2,080 people from Sandwip went abroad in 2025.
target_section: Is there a job for someone with no skills?
why_new: Local numbers only; included for completeness.

claim: The state minister for expatriates' welfare said on 30 July 2026 that most of the country's roughly three thousand recruiting licence holders are involved in irregularities, and that if the rules were properly followed no more than four or five hundred licences would survive; he also said many agencies renew their licences without being qualified to.
target_section: Is there a list of good agencies?
why_new: The minister's own estimate of how many licensed agencies would pass their licence conditions; supports the guide's point that a valid licence proves little.

claim: A Prothom Alo guide for migrant workers published on 7 July 2025 said the Probashi Kallyan Bank migration loan needs no collateral and requires the applicant's photo, voter ID, address, certificates and copies of the passport, visa and smart card, the papers of one guarantor and three bank cheques, and that an account must first be opened at the bank.
placement: other: papers for the PKB loan
why_new: Lists the papers and the three cheques; note it says one guarantor where the guide (F0116) says two, so this needs checking against PKB before use.

claim: The same guide said the PKB loan is up to Tk 3 lakh for both a new visa and a re-entry visa, with terms of 3 years and 2 years respectively, repaid in monthly instalments after a two-month grace period at 9 percent simple interest.
why_new: Adds the re-entry visa loan, its 2-year term and the two-month grace period to what the guide gives.

claim: Rawnak Jahan, a senior officer of Probashi Kallyan Bank's Cumilla region, said in April 2026 that the bank has only 4 branches for Cumilla's 17 upazilas, that the Tomsom Bridge branch has three staff and must serve 9 upazilas, and that shortage of staff and limited operations cause problems in giving and recovering loans in many cases.
why_new: Why the government loan is hard to get in one of the biggest migrant districts: branch and staff numbers from the bank itself.

claim: At the Mymensingh regional passport office, a passport application submitted through a dalal is called a "channel file" (চ্যানেল ফাইল): three dalals told Prothom Alo in 2024, on condition of anonymity, that every shop outside the office now does channel files for Tk 2,500 above the government fee, of which Tk 1,200 goes to the passport office and the rest to the dalals.
why_new: The trade term, the street price and the split between dalal and office; the guide has only TIB survey averages.

claim: The three dalals said a fake "nationality and character certificate" in the name of Mymensingh City Corporation is attached to a channel file with a special code on it, that the clerk taking applications knows from the code whose dalal sent it and accepts it without scrutiny, that the passport office keeps a daily count of coded forms, and that an office employee collects the money by that count every Wednesday.
why_new: The exact marking and weekly settlement system between dalals and office staff.

claim: On 4 May 2024 a Prothom Alo reporter saw the application of Hashem Ali of Phulpur, Mymensingh, accepted without any scrutiny at the Mymensingh regional passport office: his "nationality and character certificate" had the ward and neighbourhood fields blank and an unidentified signature, and carried a handwritten code of three capital English letters and the number 53 beside the serial number, a code the report says is given by the passport dalal.
why_new: An observed, dated instance of the code system working at the counter.

claim: There are at least 30 shops in front of the Mymensingh regional passport office in Maskanda that openly do computer typing, photocopying and online passport applications, and almost all secretly act as the office's dalals; the dalals said they used to roam in front of the office for customers but changed method because of occasional raids by the administration, and by their account at least Tk 5 lakh a day is taken from ordinary people this way.
why_new: Where the dalals sit now (shops, not the gate) and the scale claimed.

claim: Azharul Islam of Tarakanda, Mymensingh, went to the Mymensingh regional passport office on 24 April 2024, waited an hour and a half in line and had his application refused over an error in his papers; he failed on two days, with new errors found each time, and refused to use a dalal; on 28 April he went to the office's deputy assistant director Bachir Ahmed and asked why his application was not being taken when all papers were in order, the officer quickly accepted it, and he got his passport on 16 May.
why_new: A case showing what worked without a dalal: going to the office's deputy assistant director; with dates from refusal to delivery.

claim: On 4 May 2024 Sabbir Ahmed of Churkhai, Mymensingh Sadar, whose application was not accepted because of an "error", said all his papers were in order but he was told to come the next day; he then went with two friends to a shop outside the office to find a dalal.
why_new: Shows how a refused applicant is pushed to the shops.

claim: The Mymensingh office's deputy director Morad Chowdhury told Prothom Alo in June 2024 that some dalal-type people stay outside the office and applicants are told to beware of them, but that he did not know of code numbers on fake City Corporation certificates or whether any staff member takes money for it, and would look into it; the deputy assistant director also said he would look into it.
why_new: The office's response; no action is reported.

claim: Ali Yusuf, secretary of the Mymensingh city unit of SUJAN (Citizens for Good Governance), told Prothom Alo in June 2024 that everyone knows nothing gets done at the passport office without a dalal, and that his nephew had recently failed for a month to submit his application and got a passport only after applying through a dalal.
why_new: A named civil-society witness with a one-month example.

claim: On 20 November 2024 people under the banner "Victims: the ordinary people of Rajshahi" formed a human chain in front of the Rajshahi divisional passport and visa office in Shalbagan against files submitted through dalals being processed first, then met the deputy director and gave one month to end the irregularities, warning of a bigger programme otherwise.
why_new: A dated public protest against dalal-first processing at a named office.

claim: Speakers at the Rajshahi protest said they had observed that the special files coming through dalals are taken straight upstairs to the room of deputy director Rozy Khandaker, who signs them, that the assistant director enters them into the computer on the same floor, and that the files then come quickly down to the ground floor for the photograph, while people who do not pay a dalal stand for hours in the long ground-floor line.
why_new: The physical route of a dalal file inside the office (floor, room, order of steps), as alleged by protesters.

claim: The Rajshahi victims said that when a file comes without a dalal the officers only look for mistakes and when it comes through a dalal nothing is checked, and that the person who enters ordinary people's passport files on the ground floor is often not at his desk, so the ordinary line does not move.
why_new: Matches the Mymensingh pattern (errors found only in non-dalal files) at a second office.

claim: Deputy director Rozy Khandaker denied all the allegations of irregularity when the Rajshahi protesters met her and asked them to show proof of corruption, and told journalists she could not speak to the media without the permission of the passport department's Director General.
why_new: The official's denial, needed alongside the allegation.

claim: According to an intelligence agency report cited by Prothom Alo, a "G-25" syndicate of passport officers was built by the then director Toufiqul Islam under the patronage of Abu Asad when he was director (administration and finance); its 24 officers became known as G-25 because they allegedly collect at least Tk 25 lakh in bribes a day, the Anti-Corruption Commission questioned its members in 2021 on the basis of the report and filed cases against some of them, and victims in Rajshahi said in November 2024 that deputy director Rozy Khandaker is known as a member.
why_new: Names the alleged officer syndicate behind passport-office bribes and the ACC action; the guide has no named syndicate for passports.

claim: At the Gazipur regional passport office in May 2025, applicants said that applying on their own meets harassment on various pretexts while through a dalal everything is done at once, for Tk 1,000 to 1,500 paid to the dalal; a Prothom Alo reporter saw people wait about an hour for document checks and two to two and a half hours for fingerprints and photo, while those paying Tk 1,000 to 1,500 more through a dalal went straight to the fingerprint and photo room.
why_new: A 2025 street price for skipping the biometric queue at a named office, observed by a reporter; TIB's survey says the biometric stage carries the highest bribe but gives no mechanism.

claim: Ariful Islam of Kapasia said he joined the line for fingerprints and photo at the Gazipur passport office at 9 am and finished at 1:30 pm, while those who had paid a dalal finished within 10 to 15 minutes of arriving.
why_new: Queue time with and without a dalal, in an applicant's words.

claim: Riad Mia of Tongi said he waited at the Gazipur passport office until 1:30 pm on a Wednesday in May 2025 without being able to submit his wife's file, came back on Thursday morning and finished after more than two hours, and that a man had asked him for Tk 1,000 to get the work done quickly, which he did not pay.
why_new: A case of the work being done without paying, at the cost of a second day.

claim: Some 25 to 30 small shops have grown up on both sides of the road in front of the Gazipur passport office, where dalals and their associates sit with computers, fill in applicants' passport forms and themselves deposit the bank fee, Prothom Alo reported in May 2025.
why_new: Shows the dalal handling the bank payment as well as the form, at a second office with the same shop set-up as Mymensingh.

claim: Nasrin Parvin, deputy director of the Gazipur regional passport office, told Prothom Alo in May 2025 that pressure of applicants had risen in recent days so it could take some time, though not two to three hours, and that dalals may have been active before but since she arrived she has not let them inside under any circumstances.
why_new: The office's response.

claim: On 13 July 2025 at the Faridpur regional passport office, two local dalals, Siam Ahmed (27) and Rashed Khan (30), took Tk 30 thousand in all from a Rohingya couple on a promise of getting them passports, then started no passport work, threatened them and beat their son-in-law when he protested, according to local sources; he went into the office and asked the Ansar guards for help, and police detained the couple, the son-in-law and the two dalals.
why_new: A dated case of passport dalals taking money from people who cannot lawfully get a passport, with the dalals detained.

claim: The officer in charge of Faridpur Kotwali police station said in July 2025 that legal action was being taken against the two detained dalals, and that the three Rohingya would be sent to a camp if they were camp residents and otherwise back to where they live.
why_new: What the police did to the dalals and to the applicants.

claim: According to his brother Nur Hossain, Zakir Hossain of Banshkhali, Chattogram, unemployed and with a criminal case at the police station, needed a police clearance to go abroad but did not apply to the police directly because of the case, and went instead to an acquaintance working at a travel agency in Banshkhali.
why_new: Shows who buys a forged PCC and why (a pending criminal case); the guide has no case.

claim: According to Nur Hossain, the acquaintance, Abdur Rahman, said he could get the police clearance for Tk 1 lakh 23 thousand; the family paid Tk 80,000 in advance on 21 July 2026 and the rest after receiving the forged certificate on 12 August 2026.
why_new: A street price for a 'fast' PCC through a broker (answers the section's Need to know), against the Tk 1,500 fee.

claim: Police said the ring took Tk 1 lakh 23 thousand from Zakir Hossain on a promise of a quick police clearance, while making the certificate and showing it on the fake website cost Tk 3,000 in all, leaving Tk 1 lakh 20 thousand as profit.
why_new: The ring's cost and margin; not in the guide.

claim: Chattogram District Superintendent of Police Masud Alam asked people going abroad not to get a police clearance through any broker or illegal middleman but to follow the set government process, and called forging officers' signatures and using a fake website and QR code to make the document believable a very serious crime.
why_new: A named official's warning.

claim: The Cumilla additional superintendent of police said in April 2026 that although there are some complaints about police clearance, people with no case against them are getting it within the set time, and that if it takes longer the matter is resolved quickly on contacting the office concerned.
why_new: The police side on clearance delays, from one district.

claim: Md Salah Uddin, deputy director of the Divisional Passport and Visa Office in Sylhet, said on 18 April 2026 that the regular-service passport fee is BDT 4,025 for five years and BDT 5,750 for ten years and the super-express fee is BDT 10,350, and that with super-express service a person who completes biometrics in the morning can get the passport in Dhaka by the afternoon.
why_new: Ten-year fee and a super-express figure not in the guide (which gives 4,025 / 6,325 / 8,625); check the 10,350 figure against the official fee table.

claim: The same passport official said a person aged 18 or over can apply with a national ID card and a person under 18 with a birth registration, paying the set fee at a bank and giving fingerprints.
why_new: Plain statement of the identity document needed by age, from a passport office head.

claim: Mobarak Hossain, assistant director of the Cox's Bazar regional passport office, said at the 6 June 2026 roundtable that since e-passports began in 2020 no passport can be issued without online verification of the national ID and birth registration data, and that the gaps which earlier let some people get more than one passport are now easily detected.
why_new: The section gives the NID-match rule but not that a second passport is now detected; relevant to brokers who offer a new passport with changed details.

claim: A T M Abu Asad, additional director general of the Department of Immigration and Passports, told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that the department has cases where one person took passports by repeatedly changing name, date of birth and other information, and that this is reducing the acceptance of Bangladeshi passports with foreign embassies and immigration authorities.
why_new: The passport authority's own statement on identity changes in passports and their effect abroad; relevant to the FAQ on agents changing a woman's age.

claim: A T M Abu Asad, additional director general of the Department of Immigration and Passports, told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that passports have been issued in a much safer way since e-passports were introduced in 2020, that passports are now issued after verifying the NID or birth registration, and that because an e-passport takes the prints of all 10 fingers, the same person can no longer get a passport under a different identity.
why_new: The section gives fees and the matching rule; it does not say that ten fingerprints now block a second passport under another name or age.

claim: A T M Abu Asad, additional director general of the Department of Immigration and Passports, told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that super express passports are being delivered within 24 hours or two days, and that the department has no scope to give a passport without valid information and documents even to someone who went abroad by an illegal route.
why_new: Adds '24 hours' for super express (the section says within 2 working days) and the rule for people abroad irregularly who need a passport.

claim: Prothom Alo reported in March 2025 that there is little activity for workers who come back: some projects were taken up after the Covid pandemic but not many workers benefit from them.
target_section: What help is there when I come back?
why_new: Sets the official list of return help against what reaches returnees.

claim: The PKB acting regional head in Sylhet said on 18 April 2026 that the bank tries to help returnees who come back having suffered losses with loans at 8 per cent interest, but that in many cases this is not succeeding.
target_section: What help is there when I come back?
why_new: The bank's own admission that its returnee loans often do not work.

claim: Dr Jahangir Hossain, director (skills standards and curriculum) of the National Skills Development Authority, told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that under the authority's agreement with Probashi Kallyan Bank, returnees who hold a skills certificate can get a collateral-free loan of up to BDT 5 lakh, that recognition of prior learning (RPL) can create upskilling and reskilling opportunities using returnees' skills, and that work has begun to bring workers in Saudi Arabia and Singapore under RPL.
target_section: What help is there when I come back?
why_new: The FAQ says PKB lends up to Tk 3 lakh without collateral; an NSDA director says a skills certificate raises the collateral-free limit to Tk 5 lakh under an NSDA-PKB agreement. Needs checking against PKB's own terms.

claim: Md Jahangir Hossain, deputy managing director of Probashi Kallyan Bank, told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that the bank has several kinds of rehabilitation loan for returnees (rehabilitation, women's rehabilitation, special rehabilitation and self-employment loans), also lends where migrants run a business at home through their families, and has lent BDT 702 crore to 24 thousand 971 people under these rehabilitation loans.
target_section: What help is there when I come back?
why_new: Names PKB's returnee loan types and the number of borrowers (24,971), from the bank itself; the FAQ gives terms but no scale beyond the 2% pandemic figure.

claim: Mahsin Hamuda, national programme officer at the ILO (International Labour Organization), told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that 94 percent of returnee workers want to become entrepreneurs after coming home but do not get loans easily because of complicated procedures and too much paperwork, and that to solve this an arrangement has now been made to give loans across the country through Karmasangsthan Bank at 7 percent interest on submission of only three documents.
target_section: What help is there when I come back?
why_new: A second lender for returnees not in the guide: Karmasangsthan Bank, 7% interest, three documents. The article does not name the three documents or the loan ceiling.

claim: Mahsin Hamuda, national programme officer at the ILO (International Labour Organization), told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that the government recently drew up a reintegration policy for returned migrant workers, that many people do not know Probashi Kallyan Bank gives loans, and that reintegration support is usually project-based and stops when the project ends.
target_section: What help is there when I come back?
why_new: Notes the new reintegration policy and why returnee support is unreliable (project-based, little known).

claim: Anwar Hossain Chowdhury, managing director of the SME Foundation, told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that the foundation is training returnees in business planning, financial literacy, the papers needed, trade licence, TIN and BSTI certificate and product markets, and that this work is still at a very early stage.
target_section: What help is there when I come back?
why_new: Another body said to train returnees (SME Foundation), described by its own head as at an early stage; no location or enrolment route is given.

claim: In two of the cases documented by Amnesty International in Saudi Arabia, the accused said they had been forced to carry banned drugs, but the court neither examined nor accepted that, Prothom Alo reported in October 2026.
placement: other: add to the drug-packet warning
why_new: Being forced to carry drugs is no defence in practice; the guide only says drug offences can carry death.

claim: Officials said the state minister for expatriates' welfare, Shafiqur Rahman Chowdhury, met heads of foreign employers in the UAE on 25 May 2024 and discussed sending more workers as motorbike riders and car drivers.
target_section: Which countries can I go to for work right now?
why_new: Which trades the government was pushing for the UAE in 2024; low priority.

claim: According to RMMRU, 9,06,355 workers went abroad from Bangladesh from January to November 2024 against 13,05,453 in the whole of 2023, and 54,696 of them were women, 6 per cent of the total and the lowest in ten years apart from the pandemic period.
target_section: Which countries can I go to for work right now?
why_new: 2024 departure totals and the women's share (dated figures).

claim: Of more than 13 lakh workers who went abroad in 2023, 77,263 were women; BMET data show the most women in one year, 121,925, went in 2017, and the yearly figure stayed above one lakh until 2019.
target_section: Which countries can a woman go to?
why_new: Yearly totals of women migrants; the FAQ gives only 2025-26 country counts.

claim: Bangladesh began sending women workers abroad in 1991; Saudi Arabia signed its agreement with Bangladesh in 2015, after Indonesia and the Philippines stopped sending domestic workers over allegations of abuse, and most Bangladeshi women migrants go to Saudi Arabia as domestic workers.
target_section: Which countries can a woman go to?
why_new: Why the Saudi domestic-worker channel opened to Bangladesh.

claim: Tipu Sultan, joint secretary general of BAIRA, told Prothom Alo in January 2024 that Saudi employers want workers quickly once they place a demand, that because of delays the women cannot be sent, and that the employers are therefore taking workers from other countries.
target_section: Which countries can a woman go to?
why_new: The agencies' association's explanation for the fall in women going.

claim: Rebeka Khan, joint secretary (Political-1) at the Home Ministry, told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that the use of modern technology at airports, including the Passenger Name Record and Advance Passenger Information systems, is being expanded to detect fake travel documents.
why_new: Names two passenger-data systems being expanded at airports to catch fake travel documents; not in the airport section.

claim: Dr Md Al-Mamunul Ansari, DIG (Operations) of the Airport Armed Police Battalion at APBn headquarters, told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that the Airport Armed Police Battalion has worked at the airport since 2013, and that the air force and police, APBn, the Special Branch's immigration police and an anti-human-trafficking investigation team currently work there.
placement: other: who works at the airport
why_new: The section lists SB immigration and the welfare desk; it does not mention APBn or an anti-trafficking investigation team at the airport.

claim: Salma Ali, chairperson of ATSEC South Asia and adviser to the Bangladesh National Women Lawyers' Association, told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that a suspicious passenger can be identified at the airport in a few minutes of observation, and that recently a young woman bound for Nepal was suspected, steps were taken, and she was rescued and brought back to the country.
why_new: The section records women stopped on Nepal trips as a problem; this is a women's-rights lawyer citing a Nepal-bound woman who, she says, was rescued. No date or details are given.

claim: Dr Md Al-Mamunul Ansari, DIG (Operations) of the Airport Armed Police Battalion at APBn headquarters, told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that during checks at immigration officers can often tell that a person travelling on a tourist visa is in fact going for work, and that they then verify and, if needed, report it or try to stop the person; if there is a case against someone, he said, the database is checked and action is taken.
why_new: A senior airport police officer stating in his own words that tourist-visa travellers judged to be going for work are stopped, and that passengers are checked against a case database.

claim: The column says that under Saudi law employers are supposed to bear the worker's visa and recruitment costs but in practice this is often not followed, and that when Malaysia recruited government-to-government (G2G) many workers went for just Tk 35,000 in airfare, a system the writer says ended because of opposition from recruiting agencies.
target_section: Who pays for the air ticket?
why_new: What a no-broker channel cost (Tk 35,000) and why, by the writer's account, it ended.

claim: RMMRU's December 2024 report said no labour migration took place in 2024 to several countries including Oman, Bahrain, the United Arab Emirates and the Maldives, and that labour migration to Italy was stalled because of forged documents and to Serbia because the server of the application process was out of order.
target_section: Why won't BMET clear workers for some countries?
why_new: Which corridors were shut in 2024 and why Italy and Serbia stalled (dated; check against the section's current list).
